interactive.title: Powers and their slopes
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens. It opens on last lesson's growing square beside a growing cube. The square has side x, and a slider for a small step h grows its side, adding two strips, each x by h, and a corner h by h, which is where 2x came from. The cube has side 2, and the same slider grows every edge by h, adding three slabs, each x by x by h, three thin rods along the edges, each x by h by h, and a tiny cube h by h by h. A readout adds the new pieces and divides by h: each slab leaves x², each rod leaves xh and the tiny cube leaves h², so it reads 3x² + 3xh + h². As h goes 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01 it reads 19, 15.25, 12.61 and 12.06, settling on 3 × 2² = 12. Next comes a graph of y = xⁿ, where xⁿ means n x's multiplied together, with a stepper for the power n from 1 to 5 and a point P you drag along the curve. The tangent at P rides with it, with a readout of its slope beside the power rule's value, n × xⁿ⁻¹, and the two agree wherever P is: for x⁴ at x = 2 both read 4 × 2³ = 32. Then y = x³ beside a curve 5 times as tall, 5x³, whose tangent at the same x is 5 times as steep: 12 and 60 at x = 2. Then y = x² with a slider that lifts the whole curve by up to 5, with the lift alone drawn as a faint flat line of slope 0; the tangent at x = 2 rides up with it and keeps its slope of 4, because every point rises by the same amount. Then 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 9 is built a term at a time, each term lighting up with its own derivative, and the tangent at x = 1 reads 15. The last screen is an optional look at the chain rule, on y = (3x + 1)². The inside, 3x + 1, climbs 3 for every 1 across. The outside squares it, so by the power rule it climbs 2 × (3x + 1) for every 1 its inside climbs. The chain rule multiplies the two rates, like the ratios of two gearboxes in line, giving 2(3x + 1) × 3 = 18x + 6; split into 3x and 1 like last lesson's square, a square of side 3x + 1 holds 9x², two strips of 3x and a corner of 1, so 9x² + 6x + 1, whose derivative, term by term, is the same 18x + 6. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the graph.
interactive.ignores: The example rules and the values of x are chosen so the numbers come out exactly. The square and the cube are drawn with a step h big enough to see the strips, slabs and rods. A side cannot be below zero, so they only picture x above zero, but multiplying out (x + h) works the same for any x, which is why the slope readout matches the rule on the left of zero too. The stepper offers whole-number powers from 1 to 5; the rule also holds for powers below zero and between whole numbers, which the slabs do not picture.

explain.text:
For any power of x there is a short rule for its derivative, so you can differentiate a whole formula built from powers without drawing a single chord. Last lesson the growing square showed why x² gives 2x: grow the side by a small step h and the area gains two strips, x by h, and a tiny corner, h by h; divide by h and shrink it, and only 2x is left. A cube shows the next power the same way. Grow every edge of a cube of side x by h and its volume, x³, gains three slabs, each x by x by h, three thin rods, each x by h by h, and one tiny cube, h by h by h. On the graph of y = x³, moving from x to x + h raises y by exactly that new volume, so the chord between them has Δy equal to the new pieces over Δx = h. Divide each piece by h: each slab leaves x², each rod leaves xh and the tiny cube leaves h², so the chord's slope is 3x² + 3xh + h². Shrink h and every piece with an h left in it shrinks away, so the slope settles on 3x². For a cube of side 2 the chord slopes for h = 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01 are 19, 15.25, 12.61 and 12.06, settling on 12, which is 3 × 2².

Put the results side by side: x gives 1, x² gives 2x and x³ gives 3x². Each time the power comes down in front and the power left on x is one less, and the reason is the same each time. xⁿ means n x's multiplied together, so growing x by h gives n brackets of (x + h) multiplied together. Multiply them out, and the pieces with a single h in them come from taking h from one bracket and x from all the rest, so there are n of them, each xⁿ⁻¹ × h. For the square those are the two strips, and for the cube the three slabs. Every other piece has h × h or more in it, so after dividing by h it still has an h and shrinks away. So the derivative of xⁿ is nxⁿ⁻¹, the [[power rule]]: bring the power down in front, then take one off the power.[^1][^2] The slabs show why for whole-number powers; the rule also holds for powers below zero and between whole numbers,[^1] and the Second Engineer syllabus asks for it with powers above and below zero.[^3] A number in front stays. 5x³ is x³ with every height 5 times bigger, so every rise between two points is 5 times bigger over the same step across, and every slope is 5 times as steep: the derivative of 5x³ is 5 × 3x² = 15x².[^4] At x = 2, x³ climbs at 12 and 5x³ at 60. Check any answer against the picture this way: forgetting to take one off the power would make 5x³ give 15x³, which is 120 at x = 2, twice the 60 the tangent shows.

Formulas are built from terms added and taken away, and each term can be done on its own. The height of a sum is the heights added, so its rise between two points is the rises added, and its slope is the slopes added: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives.[^5] A number on its own, a [[constant]], draws a flat line, so its slope is 0.[^6] Adding a constant to a formula lifts every point of its graph by the same amount, which changes no slope. Taking a term away is adding it with a minus in front, and that minus is a number in front, so it stays. And x on its own is a straight line of slope 1, so 7x gives 7, as straight lines did last lesson. Put together, 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 9 gives 12x² − 4x + 7: 4 × 3x², then −2 × 2x, then 7, then 0.[^7] The Second Engineer syllabus asks for exactly this, the derivatives of formulas with several terms.[^8] At x = 1 that curve is at height 0 but climbing at 12 − 4 + 7 = 15. A formula with one rule inside another, such as (3x + 1)², needs one more rule, the chain rule: the outside's rate, worked out at the inside, times the inside's rate.[^9] **To differentiate a formula in powers of x, take each term on its own, multiply its number by its power and take one off the power, and let any constant give 0.[^1][^5][^6]**

analogy.text: Lay square floor tiles in a square patch 20 tiles each way, 400 tiles. To make it 21 each way you add a row of 20 along one side, a row of 20 along the other and 1 tile in the corner: 41 tiles, close to 2 × 20. Stack blocks into a cube 20 each way and a layer on three of its faces adds about 3 × 20 × 20 = 1,200 blocks. That is the power rule's 2x and 3x², counted in tiles and blocks.
analogy.breaks: Tiles and blocks come whole, so the step is at least one tile, and the corner tile and the edge blocks never shrink away: 41, not 40, and 9,261 − 8,000 = 1,261, not 1,200. The derivative lets the step shrink as small as you like, so those extra pieces shrink to nothing and the rate is exactly 2x or 3x².

practice.text:
- Write the formula as terms added and taken away: each one a number times a power of x, or a number on its own.
- For each power term, multiply the number in front by the power, then take one off the power.
- A term in x alone gives its number; a constant gives 0.
- Keep each term's sign and write the results together.
- Put in a value of x to get the rate there, in the y unit per x unit.
- To check, work out a chord with a small step: its slope should be just off your answer.

**Rules of thumb:** the new power is one less than the old. A number in front stays and multiplies. A constant drops out, because lifting a graph tilts nothing.

**Worked example:** The heat given off in a conductor is P = I²R watts. Take its resistance as a fixed 2 Ω, say. Then P = 2I², so dP/dI = 2 × 2I = 4I watts per amp. At 10 A the heat is 2 × 10² = 200 W, and it is growing at 4 × 10 = 40 W per amp, twice the average of 200 ÷ 10 = 20 W per amp from 0 A. Check with a chord: at 10.1 A the heat is 2 × 10.1² = 204.02 W, 4.02 W more, and 4.02 ÷ 0.1 = 40.2 W per amp, just above 40.

**Common mistakes**
- Forgetting to take one off the power: 5x³ gives 15x², not 15x³.
- Dropping the number in front: 5x³ gives 15x², not 3x².
- Keeping a constant: the − 9 in 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 9 gives 0.
- Leaving the x on a straight-line term: 7x gives 7, not 7x.
- Reading the height as the slope: at x = 1, 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 9 is at 0 but climbing at 15.

interactive.html:
A growing square and cube, then curves built from powers of x, each with a tangent whose slope is worked out from its rule.

Every slope and volume here is worked out from each screen's own rule.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the cube's new volume shrinking to just its three slabs, so the slope settles on 3x², the power rule's n × xⁿ⁻¹ for n = 3, when you shrink the step h.

checks.label: The derivative of the power xⁿ is nxⁿ⁻¹: for every power n from 1 to 5 and every half step P can be dragged to, the tangent drawn through P has the slope the chords there settle on from either side, and the working sets it beside n × xⁿ⁻¹, the same number

The derivative of a constant multiplied by a function is the constant multiplied by the derivative: at every x P can reach, the tangent on the curve 5 times as tall as y = x³ is 5 times as steep as the one on y = x³, 12 and 60 at x = 2, and the working says 5x³ gives 15x²

The derivative of a constant function is zero: each lift from 0 to 5 is a flat line of slope 0, so the lifted curve's tangent at x = 2 still climbs 4 for every 1 across, through P raised by the lift; and y = x² + 9 has the slope of x² at x = 3, 6

The derivative of the sum of two functions is the sum of their derivatives: at x = 1 the terms of 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 9 have slopes 12, −4, 7 and 0, which add to the 15 of the tangent drawn there; and on every puzzle curve the slope at P is its terms' slopes added

From the rules, by hand: a cube of side 2 grows by 19, 7.625, 1.261 and 0.120601 for h = 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01, so its chord slopes are 19, 15.25, 12.61 and 12.06, settling on 3 × 2² = 12; side 4 cm grows at 48 cm³ per cm (volume 64 cm³, one slab 16); x⁴ at 2 has slope 32; x⁵ at 2 has 80 (slips 160 and 16); x³ and 5x³ at 2 are 8 and 40 high, with slopes 12 and 60, and 15x³ would give 120; 4x³ at 2 has 48 (slips 16 and 96); x² has slope 4 at 2; x² + 9 at 3 has 6 (slips 15 and 18); 4x³ − 2x² + 7x − 9 is 0 at 1, with slope 15; 2x³ + 5x² − 3x + 8 at 2 has 41 (slips 82 and 49); x³ + 2x at 2 s is 12 m, going 14 m per s (slip 16); (3x + 1)² at 1 has slope 2 × 4 × 3 = 24, as 18x + 6 gives; and the screens' sentences quote these same values

The growing cube of side 2: at every stop of the slider it shows three slabs, three rods and one tiny cube, which together are (2 + h)³ − 8; divided by h they leave 12, 6h and h², which the bar draws to scale and the table adds up to the chord slope

The derivative of a composite function is the outer function's derivative at the inner function times the inner function's derivative: on y = (3x + 1)², at every half step from 0 to 1.5 the slope is 2(3x + 1) × 3, the same as 9x² + 6x + 1 gives term by term, and the tangent drawn at x = 1 climbs 24

Every puzzle offers three different answers and accepts only the right one; each wrong answer is the slip it stands for: 64 cm³ and 16 cm³ per cm against 48 cm³ per cm; 16 and 160 against 80; 16 and 96 against 48; 15 and 18 against 6; 6x³ + 10x² − 3x (82 at P) and 6x² + 10x + 5 (49 at P) against 6x² + 10x − 3; 12 m and 16 m per s against 14 m per s

Before an answer no puzzle shows it: no tangent, nothing red, and the working ends in a question mark; a right answer shows its value and the tangent with nothing red, and every wrong answer shows its slip in red
Dragging P keeps it on a half step inside its range: −1.5 to 2 on the powers, 0.5 to 2.5 on the curve 5 times as tall
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 1.3 s

applied.problem: The opening says the power rule lets you differentiate "a whole formula", but it covers only formulas built from powers of x; later sine waves (i10) and brackets like (3x + 1)² need more than term-by-term powers.

"A real conductor's resistance rises a little as it warms" is too general: it holds for metals (and the rise is not always little over a big warming), while carbon and semiconductors fall as they warm.
